questions.stem: What does data sovereignty require of an organisation's data?
options: That it is encrypted before it is analysed
That it is accessed only by database administrators
That it remains within the country or defined boundary where it was generated
That it is copied to at least two cloud regions
That it is deleted once it is no longer needed
questions.explanation: Data sovereignty means keeping data within defined boundaries: if data is generated in Singapore, it should remain within the borders of Singapore.

questions.stem: Which two terms are described as being very near to data sovereignty?
options: Data security and data privacy
Data quality and data lineage
Data warehousing and data mining
Data masking and data subsetting
Data encoding and data encryption
questions.explanation: Data sovereignty is introduced as a term very near to data security and data privacy, which make sure data is accessed only by those who need it or own it.

questions.stem: Within an organisation, what does an ACL (Access Control List) record?
options: The countries in which each data set may be stored
The list of users and the level of access each may have on certain data sets
The encryption keys assigned to each database
The audit history of every query run against the data
The cloud vendors approved for hosting data
questions.explanation: An ACL records all the users together with the level of access they can have on certain data sets, such as developers, DBAs, managers, business users and cost-centre staff.

questions.stem: In an on-premises infrastructure, how must employees access company applications from home?
options: Through a public web portal
By downloading a local copy of the data
By emailing the database administrator for an extract
By logging in via a VPN (Virtual Private Network)
By using any BI tool with their normal password
questions.explanation: In an on-premises solution data is not allowed to leave the network, so employees working from home must log in via a VPN to minimise the risk of losing data.

questions.stem: What does an organisation do in a cloud solution instead of buying its own hardware and servers?
options: It shares hardware with other companies in its own data centre
It builds a private network across several offices
It rents storage and processing from vendors such as Amazon, Microsoft or Google
It stores all data on employee laptops
It outsources its ACL to a regulator
questions.explanation: In the cloud, organisations do not need to buy hardware or servers; they rent them from vendors such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Oracle, IBM or Ali Baba.

questions.stem: In the Singapore and Azure example, why does using a cloud service make data sovereignty a question mark?
options: Because Azure does not support access control lists
Because the customer's data would leave Singapore and be stored in a USA data centre
Because Microsoft charges more for customers outside the USA
Because cloud data cannot be encrypted
Because Singapore has no data privacy laws
questions.explanation: Azure belongs to a USA-based company, so a Singapore customer's data would leave the Singapore border and be stored in a USA data centre, breaching the boundary rule.

questions.stem: How are cloud vendors responding to the data sovereignty problem?
options: By refusing customers from regulated sectors
By encrypting all data before it crosses a border
By opening data centres in different countries
By letting customers host the vendor's software on-premises only
By asking regulators to remove border restrictions
questions.explanation: To cater to the data sovereignty problem statement, vendors are opening data centres in different countries so data can stay within its own region.

questions.stem: Which activity does the author argue cannot realistically be restricted under data sovereignty?
options: Storing data in a vendor's overseas data centre
Viewing data from across a border
Granting developers access to production data
Renting cloud servers from a foreign vendor
Backing up data outside the country
questions.explanation: The author's view is that storage must stay within defined boundaries, but viewing cannot be limited, because opening the World Wide Web already means going cross-border.

questions.stem: What is the recommended solution for keeping data sovereign while still using it globally?
options: Store data in your own region and access it via any BI tool from anywhere
Keep all data on-premises and forbid remote access
Store a copy of the data in every country where users sit
Use only vendors headquartered in your own country
Replace cloud services with paper records
questions.explanation: The suggested approach is to store data within your own region or defined boundaries and access it through any BI tool anywhere in the world.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed among the roles that may be given different levels of data access in an organisation's ACL?
options: Developers
Database administrators
Department managers
Business users
External auditors
questions.explanation: The example roles are developers, database administrators, department managers, business users and cost-centre staff; external auditors are not mentioned.
